title: Associations of post-migration difficulties and religious coping with psychological distress among Syrian refugee youth
abstract: Background: Syrian refugee youth in Jordan experience persistent post-migration difficulties that may affect psychological well-being. Religious coping represents a culturally relevant response to adversity, although its relationship with psychological distress remains unclear. Objective: To examine the associations of post-migration living difficulties (PMLD) and positive and negative religious coping with psychological distress among Syrian refugee youth in Jordan. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 460 Syrian refugees aged 15–29 years residing in refugee camps and host communities in Jordan. Data were collected between August and September 2025 using the Arabic PMLD Scale, Brief Religious Coping Scale, and Brief Symptom Inventory-53. Multivariable linear regression examined associations with psychological distress, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Separate interaction models examined the moderating roles of positive and negative religious coping. Results: The mean PMLD score was 35.20 ± 4.95, with financial hardship, difficulties obtaining financial assistance, family-related concerns, and employment challenges receiving the highest ratings. Positive religious coping was more frequently reported than negative religious coping (19.01 ± 3.00 vs. 8.08 ± 3.29). The mean raw Global Severity Index (GSI) was 1.47 ± 0.17. PMLD was not significantly correlated with GSI (r = −0.022, p = .637). In the adjusted regression model, PMLD (p = 0.351), positive religious coping (p = 0.345), and negative religious coping (p = 0.848) were not significantly associated with GSI. Neither positive (p = 0.860) nor negative religious coping (p = 0.190) significantly moderated the PMLD–GSI association. Conclusion: Post-migration adversity and religious coping were not independently associated with psychological distress in this sample. Findings should be interpreted cautiously given limitations in measurement reliability. Culturally responsive psychosocial services should consider both psychological needs and persistent socioeconomic challenges affecting refugee youth.
